# Observability of Isolated Agents

How to monitor sandboxed AI agents without weakening security boundaries.

## The Core Tension

Observability typically requires network access (send metrics to collector), filesystem access (write logs), or agent-side instrumentation (install monitoring libraries). All three weaken isolation. The solution: observe from outside the boundary or use indirection layers that the agent never controls.

## Architecture: Hooks as Indirection [21]

The Claude Code hooks pattern solves this elegantly:

```
Agent (sandboxed) → Tool call → Hook fires (host process) → HTTP POST → SQLite → WebSocket → Dashboard
```

The agent never gets network access to monitoring infrastructure. Hooks execute as subprocess commands within Claude Code's engine context — they inherit the host user's credentials, not the agent's sandbox [21].

**12 event types captured** [21]:
- PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PostToolUseFailure
- PermissionRequest, Notification
- UserPromptSubmit, Stop
- SubagentStart, SubagentStop
- PreCompact, SessionStart, SessionEnd

**Metrics tracked** [21]:
- Per-agent: source app, agent type, model selection, session lifecycle
- Tool-level: names, inputs, results, MCP server detection, failure states
- Subagent coordination: agent IDs, team membership, transcript paths, completion status
- User interaction: notification types, permission requests, prompt content

**Storage**: SQLite with WAL mode for concurrent access. Handles multi-agent sessions writing simultaneously [21].

**Visualization**: WebSocket broadcast to Vue.js client. Dual-color system distinguishes concurrent sessions (app color for left border, session color for second border) [21].

## eBPF-Based Container Observability [34]

For scenarios where hooks aren't available (non-Claude agents, or when `--bare` skips hooks):

**Tetragon** [34]: eBPF-based security observability and runtime enforcement. Observes containerized workloads at the kernel level without installing anything inside the container.

Properties:
- No agent-side instrumentation required
- Kernel-level visibility into syscalls, network connections, file access
- Policy enforcement (can block actions, not just observe)
- Works with any containerized workload regardless of runtime

**Kata Containers + eBPF** (discovery): Ant Group uses this combination at scale — strong VM isolation with eBPF-based observability for policy enforcement.

**Limitation**: eBPF operates at the syscall level, not the semantic level. It can see "process opened file X" but not "Claude Code edited function Y." Semantic observability still requires hooks or structured output parsing.

## OTel GenAI Semantic Conventions [22][23]

The emerging standard for agent tracing:

**Agent span attributes** [23]:
- `gen_ai.agent.id` — unique agent identifier
- `gen_ai.agent.name` — human-readable name
- `gen_ai.agent.description` — role description
- `gen_ai.agent.version` — version string
- `gen_ai.conversation.id` — session/conversation identifier
- `gen_ai.operation.name` — required; operation being performed
- `gen_ai.provider.name` — required; model provider
- `gen_ai.tool.type` — Extension (API call) / Function (client-side) / Datastore (RAG)

**Metrics** [23]:
- `gen_ai.client.token.usage` — histogram, `{token}` unit
- `gen_ai.client.operation.duration` — histogram, seconds
- **No cost metric defined** — cost must be derived from token counts + per-model pricing at application layer

**Convention status** [22]:
- Agent application conventions: Finalized (based on Google AI agent whitepaper)
- Agent framework conventions (CrewAI, AutoGen, LangGraph): Still being defined
- Agentic systems conventions: Open issue (#2664), in progress

**Datadog support**: Native ingestion of OTel GenAI conventions from v1.37+ (discovery).

## Anomaly Detection [33]

Five anomaly categories for multi-agent systems:

| Category | Signals | Detection |
|----------|---------|-----------|
| Behavioral | Action distribution shifts, tool selection changes | Baseline comparison |
| Communication | Message storms, deadlocks between agents | Rate monitoring |
| Resource | CPU/memory spikes, token usage anomalies | Threshold alerts |
| Performance | Latency increases, accuracy drops | Trend analysis |
| Emergent | Cross-agent patterns not visible per-agent | Aggregate analysis |

**Loop detection** [33]: Monitor agent tool selection patterns — unnecessary retries and identical tool calls indicate stuck agents.

**Drift signals** (discovery): Token usage spikes, off-target outputs, rising escalation rates for specific input categories. Distribution shift detected via KS test or Population Stability Index.

**No quantified default thresholds** — all are context-dependent baselines that must be established per deployment [33].

## Observability Without Network Access

For fully network-isolated containers (`--network none`):

| Approach | Mechanism | Limitations |
|----------|-----------|-------------|
| Hooks (host-side) | Claude Code engine fires hooks outside container | Only for Claude Code; requires hook config |
| Log volume mount | Mount log directory writable; host reads it | Agent can write anything to log volume |
| eBPF (host-side) | Kernel observes container syscalls | Syscall-level only; no semantic understanding |
| Exit code + structured output | Parse agent's stdout/stderr after completion | Post-hoc only; no real-time |
| Filesystem artifact polling | Check for completion files periodically | Simple but high-latency [28] |

The `dev-and-ai-tools` approach [43]: Relies on structured output parsing (YAML verdicts from judge) and filesystem state files (`BUILD_STATUS.md`, `TASK_LIST.md`). Container logs provide forensic detail. No real-time streaming during execution.

## Git Status Monitoring Across Worktrees

For parallel agents in separate worktrees:

- **dmux** [29]: Built-in status across all panes/worktrees
- **Webmux** [42]: Real-time dashboard combining worktree status with agent activity
- **agtx** [28]: Artifact polling per phase with visual status (spinner → checkmark)
- **gwq** (discovery): Table-view status with watch mode, JSON/CSV output, tmux integration

## Gaps and Limitations

- **OTel has no guidance** for air-gapped/network-isolated monitoring scenarios [22]
- **Hook events can be lost** if container is killed mid-execution before PostToolUse fires (no documented mitigation) [21]
- **eBPF overhead** for AI agent monitoring is not quantified in published sources [34]
- **No standardized cost metric** in OTel — every implementation must derive cost from tokens × price [23]
- **`--bare` mode skips hooks** [14], eliminating the primary observability mechanism for headless execution
